This is a pilot vignette, to be revised and extended. It fits the model from
`vignette("flexyBayes-01-mixed-models")` and shows what a Bayesian fit adds.

# Point estimates and distributions

REML returns a point estimate and a standard error for each variance
component. A Bayesian fit returns a posterior distribution for each one.
Intervals, heritabilities and comparisons between genotypes are all computed
from that distribution.

# The prior

The prior states which values a parameter can plausibly take before the data
are seen. The posterior combines the prior with the likelihood. By default
flexyBayes puts a half-normal prior on every standard deviation, scaled to the
response. `prior_summary()` shows what it chose:


``` r
fit <- flexybayes(
  fixed   = yield ~ rep,
  random  = ~ rep:block + gen,
  data    = john.alpha,
  backend = "inla",
  verbose = FALSE
)

prior_summary(fit)
#> <prior_summary>  backend = inla
#>   Source: auto-default half-normal on SD (weakly informative, no upper bound)
#>     Scale s        = 3.049069 (in the units of the response)
#>     Scale basis    = identity_sd_half_normal
#>     prior_fixed_sd:  not supplied -- the fixed effects carry INLA's own control.fixed defaults -- prec = 0.001 (a standard deviation near 32, in standard deviations of the response on a Gaussian identity-link fit), and prec.intercept = 0, which is flat
#> 
#> <fb_prior> 3 specifications
#>   sigma ~ half_normal(scale = 3.049069)  -> family:INLA.Data1:theta1
#>   sd(group = "rep:block") ~ half_normal(scale = 3.049069)  -> random:rep_block_id:theta
#>   sd(group = "gen") ~ half_normal(scale = 3.049069)  -> random:gen:theta
#> 
#>   As each engine slot received it (read back from the fit):
#>     the fit runs on the standardised response, so a bound or scale
#>     on a standard deviation is the stated one divided by the
#>     response scale 0.609814
#>     family:INLA.Data1:theta1  <prior: half-normal-SD(5) on the standardised response = half-normal-SD(3.049) on the response>  [sigma:sigma]  read back as sent
#>     random:rep_block_id:theta  <prior: half-normal-SD(5) on the standardised response = half-normal-SD(3.049) on the response>  [sd:rep:block]  read back as sent
#>     random:gen:theta  <prior: half-normal-SD(5) on the standardised response = half-normal-SD(3.049) on the response>  [sd:gen]  read back as sent
#>     3 further slots carry the engine's own prior (listed in `$slots`)
```

A different prior gives a different answer. With many levels per variance
component the difference is small. With few levels it can be large, and the
prior should then be chosen with care (see `?fb_prior`).

# The posterior


``` r
summary(fit)$varcomp[, c("component", "estimate", "conf.low", "conf.high")]
#>      component  estimate  conf.low conf.high
#> 1        sigma 0.2925200 0.2288441 0.3713359
#> 2 sd_rep:block 0.2878226 0.1630016 0.4669522
#> 3       sd_gen 0.3970952 0.2733145 0.5602157
```

`estimate` is the posterior mean. `conf.low` and `conf.high` bound a 95%
credible interval: given the model and the prior, the parameter lies inside
it with probability 0.95.

# Functions of the parameters

In REML, a heritability and its standard error come from the delta method,
which assumes approximate normality. Near a boundary this can give an
interval below zero or above one.

Here the heritability is computed on each posterior draw, so every draw, and
therefore the interval, lies between 0 and 1:


``` r
h2 <- vpredict(fit, h2 ~ sd_gen^2 / (sd_gen^2 + sigma^2), draws = TRUE)
range(h2[, "h2"])
#> [1] 0.2473929 0.8876038
quantile(h2[, "h2"], c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
#>      2.5%       50%     97.5% 
#> 0.4319658 0.6424342 0.8208294
```

# Variances near zero

REML can estimate a variance component as exactly zero, which reads as
certainty that the effect is absent. When the whole credible interval of a
standard deviation lies close to zero, flexyBayes warns, names the term, and
suggests reporting it as not identified rather than as zero.

# Small trials

With many levels, the posterior mean is close to the REML estimate and the
credible interval is close to the Wald interval. With few levels they
differ. `vignette("flexyBayes-04-illustration")` shows this on a trial
reduced in size.

# Run time

INLA approximates the posterior and returns in seconds. brms samples it with
Stan and takes minutes. The printed fit names the engine that was used.
